name: Louisiana
summary_text: Louisiana stands under the United States national framework on travel documents and entry. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker inconsistent with sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. The Supreme Court allowed these restrictions to take effect in November 2025, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992, and the American Civil Liberties Union's suit on behalf of seven plaintiffs remains in federal court. By March 2025 trans and nonbinary travellers reported passports being confiscated or blocked at processing, with some left stranded abroad. Entry screening carries separate exposure. Since 25 February 2025 the State Department has flagged visa applicants with an internal marking, treating as fraud, with a permanent bar, any applicant listing a gender other than the one assigned at birth, in the context of barring trans athletes from entering the United States to compete in women's sports. Separately, Transportation Security Administration checkpoint procedures involve secondary screening, hand-held devices and pat-downs that can be invasive of privacy and risk outing a trans traveller. Louisiana records the highest per-capita killing rate of trans women of any state in the country: 24.7 per 100,000 people per year reported, on 19 recorded victims, against 23.5 for the state ranked safest. The count rests on a base of 428 victims recorded across the United States between 2008 and 2025, and every figure in that base is an undercount floor. A national analysis drawing on that data cautions that rankings built on legal risk do not sort physical safety: the states holding the worst law carry the highest rate. Violence in Louisiana has also produced prosecutions of the people attacked. In August 2026 a mob beat trans couple Aurora Rush and Shae Sanders over restroom use at Cypress Black Bayou Park in Benton. Sanders, who has a pre-existing spinal injury, and Rush, who suffered a concussion and blood pooling, were both charged with disturbing the peace while no attacker was arrested, and the Sheriff's Office reported no other arrests that day. Rush was denied hospital care, jailed in a men's facility and searched by a male guard despite a 'female' marker on her driver's licence. The plea deal offered to the victims was not signed. The same municipality simultaneously voted one of the country's most severe anti-trans restroom ordinances, placing local restroom access for trans residents and visitors on a restrictive footing at the time of the attack. Custody is a documented site of harm. On 2 April 2024 Yella (Robert) Clark Jr., a 45-year-old Black trans woman serving a life sentence at Angola prison, was killed in a fight with several inmates. She was at least the 16th trans or gender-expansive person killed that year and the fifth in April alone, and such deaths are systematically under- or mis-reported.

sources.title: 2023 Louisiana ban on gender-affirming healthcare for minors / 2022 transgender sports ban
sources.documents: State Senate passed June 5, 2023 bill to ban puberty blockers, hormones, surgeries for minors effective Jan 1, 2024; Governor Edwards vetoed 3 bills June 2023, Legislature overrode in July 2023 to enact healthcare ban; 2021 sports bill passed House 77-17 Senate 29-6 vetoed as discrimination, veto override failed by 2 votes; June 2022 ban on transgender girls in public-school sports passed with veto-proof two-thirds so Gov. John Bel Edwards did not veto; insurance/Medicaid do not cover transition care.

name: Maine
summary_text: Maine is a comparatively low-risk state for a transgender visitor within the United States. A July 2026 national anti-trans legal risk assessment places Maine in its Low-Risk States group. The sources reviewed attribute to Maine none of the state-level document restrictions, facility bans or care bans documented elsewhere: no state law blocking marker changes, no state bathroom restriction and no state ban on gender-affirming care is recorded against Maine in this inventory.  The federal layer nevertheless governs a visitor in Maine in full. Under Executive Order 14168 of January 2025, federal identity documents must reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, new passport applications are decided as M or F on supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X remain valid only until expiry. The Supreme Court allowed those restrictions to take effect in November 2025. Screening at US checkpoints can require secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that out a traveller, and visa applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex risk refusal as fraud, with a February 2025 ban on trans athletes entering to compete in women's sport.  Maine's favourable state posture does not insulate institutions from federal enforcement. In March 2025 the University of Maine System announced compliance with federal restrictions on transgender sports participation after the US Department of Agriculture suspended federal funding for research and programmes while investigating possible sex-based discrimination in federally funded education programmes. The July 2026 assessment separately flags Maine's risk as increased on that basis, the only factor cited against the state.  Maine Corrections houses transgender prisoners by current gender identity. Andrea Balcer, a 27-year-old transgender woman convicted of two murders, was being held in the women's facility at the Maine Correctional Center in Windham for at least a year as of April 2026. On 3 April 2026 another inmate, Katie Mountain, 41, filed a 30-page complaint in state court against Maine Department of Corrections Commissioner Randall Liberty, Warden Ben Beal and Balcer, alleging chronic harassment and assault by the transgender prisoner. Attorney Cynthia Dill filed the complaint. The placement is documented; the harassment and assault claims are allegations, and no ruling has been reported.  Federal custody and care policies apply within the state's federal facilities and to federally funded providers. The Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted conversion-therapy-style policies for transgender inmates from 2026 and stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held in 2025; the Department of Justice subpoenaed records of patients under 19 from more than 20 hospitals in summer 2025; and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court, with the outcome of individual cases unresolved.
